method: AI-assisted desk research from manufacturer archives. Editorial comparisons are interpretations, not road-test findings.

profiles.name: Ferrari F40
profiles.idea: Turbo power and a steel structure reinforced with composites
profiles.photo: F40 reference photograph; exact build year is not verified.
profiles.title: Why the F40 still makes you stop scrolling
profiles.intro: A wing, a red body and a familiar silhouette can make the F40 feel like a logo. Look past that familiarity: this is a useful starting point for understanding how materials and engine choices shape a sports car.
sections: The decision behind the shape

Ferrari introduced the F40 for its fortieth anniversary in 1987. Its own archive describes a twin-turbo V8 and a tubular steel structure combined with composite reinforcement. Pininfarina shaped a body with prominent air intakes and a rear wing. Those are connected engineering choices, rather than three unrelated styling flourishes.
What to look for in a photograph

Start at the side intakes, then follow the body towards the rear wing. Ask where air enters, where heat must leave, and which surfaces might manage airflow. A photograph can help you frame these questions; it cannot tell you how well a particular car performs.
A better comparison than a horsepower contest

Compare the F40 with the Miura and the original NSX. The interesting difference is each project’s approach to packaging and construction: transverse V12, turbocharged V8 with composites, and an aluminium body structure. That comparison gives you something to notice even when you never expect to drive any of them.
profiles.question: How did the engineering choices change the shape?

profiles.name: Lamborghini Miura
profiles.idea: A sideways engine package to shorten the wheelbase
profiles.photo: Miura P400 S reference photograph; the story discusses the wider Miura family.
profiles.title: The Miura’s most interesting detail is under the body
profiles.intro: Before you call it beautiful, ask how all that machinery fits. The Miura makes more sense when you imagine the car from above, with its engine sitting sideways behind the seats.
sections: Turn the engine, change the package

Lamborghini’s history records the Miura’s Geneva debut in March 1966. Its V12 sat behind the cockpit and ahead of the rear wheels. Mounting it transversely helped shorten the wheelbase, while the gearbox presented a packaging challenge. Bertone supplied the body. The low silhouette is the visible result of choices hidden underneath it.
One name, several versions

The manufacturer distinguishes the original P400, the later P400 S and the SV. The catalogue photograph here is labelled P400 S. That matters: treating every Miura photograph as the same specification would erase the changes made during the model’s life. Save the nameplate, then check the version when you need a precise fact.
Try this next time you see one

Find a side view and mark three points mentally: the seating area, the rear axle and the engine compartment. Now look at an F40. Both put their engine behind the cabin, but that does not make their packaging identical. Comparing the arrangement is more revealing than repeating a supercar ranking.
profiles.question: Where does the engine sit, and what does that let the designer do?
sources: Debut, transverse V12 layout and P400 / S / SV sequence.

profiles.name: Mazda MX-5
profiles.idea: A two-seat roadster with a manually operated soft top
profiles.photo: Later MX-5 RF shown. It is not the original NA discussed in this story.
profiles.title: The MX-5 makes a case for choosing less
profiles.intro: What if a sports car starts with the experience you want, rather than the largest engine you can fit? Mazda’s original MX-5 development story is a useful answer to that question.
sections: The layout was a choice

Mazda considered front-wheel drive, a rear-wheel-drive layout and a mid-engine proposal. It selected a front-engine, rear-wheel-drive two-seat roadster. The original car used a naturally aspirated 1.6-litre four-cylinder engine and double-wishbone suspension. A powerplant frame connected the transmission and differential. These details belong to the original design, not every later MX-5.
The roof tells you about the brief

Mazda’s account describes a manually operated soft top and two seats rather than a two-plus-two arrangement. Those decisions help explain the brief: make a compact open car around its occupants. They do not establish that every driver will fit comfortably, or that every used example is a good purchase.
Make the comparison personal

If you are exploring the idea of owning a roadster, list the things a photograph cannot settle: your seating position, luggage needs, roof operation and where the car will live. Test those in person before choosing a version. For browsing, compare the MX-5’s compact open-car brief with the M3’s production-car racing brief.
profiles.question: Which compromises would make the car more enjoyable for you?
sources: Competing layout proposals and the selected roadster brief.
Original engine, suspension, powerplant frame, seating and soft top.

profiles.name: BMW M3
profiles.idea: A road model developed around Group A racing requirements
profiles.photo: Later M3 CS shown. It is not the original E30 discussed in this story.
profiles.title: Why the first M3 does not explain every M3
profiles.intro: The badge survived. The engineering brief changed. Start with the original E30 to understand why reading “M3” on a listing is only the beginning of identifying the car.
sections: The first brief came from racing

BMW’s E30 history describes a 1986 launch and Group A homologation rules requiring 5,000 road cars within twelve months. The original M3 used a naturally aspirated 2.3-litre four-cylinder engine. Wider arches, a rear wing and changes around the rear roof area were part of the E30’s distinctive body treatment. A 1990 Sport Evolution used a 2.5-litre engine.
Do not carry those facts into another generation

Later M3 generations changed engines and body arrangements. The M3 CS photograph on this page shows a much later car. Its presence in the catalogue does not make the original E30’s engine or racing context apply to it. Compare the scope labels before comparing the facts.
A more useful way to browse the badge

Build a shortlist around the reason you care: the original racing story, a particular body shape, or the idea of an everyday performance car. Then identify the generation and exact variant. Engine specifications, inspection needs and running costs require that second step; this historical profile is not a shortcut around it.
profiles.question: Are you interested in the badge, or one particular generation?

profiles.name: Honda NSX
profiles.idea: An aluminium body structure paired with everyday-use goals
profiles.photo: Second-generation NC1 NSX shown. It is not the original NSX discussed in this story.
profiles.title: The NSX asks a different supercar question
profiles.intro: A dramatic car can also be designed around the person who has to use it. Honda’s original NSX project is interesting because its goals included comfort and safety alongside performance.
sections: Construction changed the factory, too

Honda’s heritage account describes an all-aluminium monocoque body and the manufacturing work needed to make it. Different aluminium alloys and production processes led to a dedicated plant in Tochigi in 1990. This was a construction project as well as a sports-car project. Honda’s original Japanese launch announcement dates the road car’s introduction to September 1990.
The ordinary-use ambition matters

Honda’s account puts comfort and safety into the development brief. Read that as a stated engineering intention, rather than proof that an ageing example is safe, dependable or comfortable for you. A manufacturer archive explains what the team aimed to achieve; it does not replace an inspection.
Put it beside the F40

Compare what each source chooses to explain. Ferrari emphasises turbo power and composite reinforcement; Honda describes an aluminium body and the manufacturing system behind it. Neither fact creates an automatic winner. Together they show that two exciting cars can answer quite different design questions. Save both and compare their project briefs.
profiles.question: What changes when everyday use is part of the original brief?
sources: Development goals, aluminium construction and dedicated factory.

profiles.name: Mercedes-Benz 300 SL
profiles.idea: Upward-opening doors made necessary by the high frame sides
profiles.photo: 300 SL reference photograph; exact build year and condition are not verified.
profiles.title: The gullwing doors solve a problem
profiles.intro: It is easy to see the doors as theatre. The more interesting story is why the engineers needed them, and why the later roadster could use a different solution.
sections: The frame comes first

Mercedes-Benz’s museum account explains that the 300 SL coupé’s tubular frame rose high at the sides. That prevented a conventional door opening, so the doors opened upwards. The road coupé, internally W198, debuted in New York in February 1954. Its racing predecessor carried the different W194 designation.
The design had consequences

The museum describes removable rectangular side windows and a steering wheel that could tilt to help occupants get in. For the 1957 roadster, Mercedes-Benz changed the frame around the entrance, allowing a lower sill and conventional front-hinged doors. The famous shape is therefore a useful example of how one structural decision can create several everyday compromises.
Look beyond the iconic angle

When browsing a car you know mainly from photographs, seek the views that answer practical questions: the opening, the sill, the cabin and the controls. Ask what the designer had to accommodate. With the 300 SL, that exercise is more informative than another claim that its doors are beautiful.
profiles.question: Which engineering constraint created the detail you remember?
sources: W198 debut, frame, doors, side windows, steering wheel and roadster changes.
